Two drains were placed, the hamstring was imbricated to obliterate dead space, and multilayered closure with compressive wrapping was performed. Within 48 hours, the fluid had reaccumulated. Approximately 1.5 L of bloody fluid was evacuated through a rind-like capsule, and small areas of solid hypertrophic tissue at the periphery were sampled. An open irrigation and debridement with biopsy was performed.

The patient is an 8-year-old boy. The patient presented with an 8-month history of painful oral ulcers. He had intermittent fever. He had no genital ulcers. He had bloody stools. He was initially treated as PFAPA with steroids, but symptoms recurred when the steroids were tapered. He had a one-time perianal ulcer. He had folliculitis on his scalp and buttocks.

Ophthalmological examination was negative, with no pathergy. On examination, there were no perianal ulcers, arthritis, or other skin findings. Abdominal examination was normal, with no tenderness or masses. On examination, he had multiple large oral ulcers on the tongue, palate, and lips.

Buccal biopsies showed chronic inflammation with granulation tissue, no granulomas, and grew Fusobacterium periodontium. Multiple endoscopies and colonoscopies with ileal intubation were negative. Capsule endoscopy, CT of the abdomen, and MRI enterography showed no abnormalities. Prometheus IBD sgi testing demonstrated a pattern consistent with Crohn's disease, with positive anti-A4-Fa2 IgG, anti-Fax IgG, ATG16L1 heterozygous, NKX2-3 heterozygous, ICAM-1, SAA 179, and elevated CRP, and negative ASCA and ANCA. An extensive workup for systemic lupus erythematosus, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, tuberculosis, cyclic neutropenia, primary immunodeficiencies, and periodic fever syndromes was unremarkable.

At month 18, a fourth colonoscopy revealed large, round ulcers in the terminal ileum with granulation tissue and chronic inflammatory infiltrates, but no granulomas or cobblestoning. Despite treatment with steroids, colchicine, infliximab, and methotrexate—later escalated to high-dose infliximab—his bloody stools worsened and he developed severe malnutrition with a BMI z-score of −2.38. After treatment was switched to ustekinumab, his gastrointestinal symptoms improved. Brain MRI/MRA/MRV revealed extensive thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, and proximal right transverse sinus. At month 19, he developed bilateral hip effusions. A lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 39 cm H2O. A hypercoagulability panel was negative. He later presented with headaches, emesis, and fevers.

The patient is a 58-year-old woman. On cycle 1 day 3, she developed neutropenic fever. She had a 4-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia treated with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. Prophylactic levofloxacin, isavuconazonium, acyclovir, and allopurinol were started for neutropenia and tumor-lysis risk.

Dermatologic examination revealed a solitary subcutaneous nodule without epidermal ulceration. She had periorbital tenderness. She had bilateral purpuric papules on the lower extremities.

A CT pulmonary angiogram showed a pulmonary embolism, small bilateral pleural effusions, and basilar atelectasis. Maxillofacial CT demonstrated maxillary sinus opacification with hyperdense material and orbital fat stranding. An initial biopsy was non-specific, showing mild inflammation but no evidence of infection, leukemic infiltration, or neutrophilic dermatosis. Bone marrow biopsy showed 2% blasts. In October 2021, her ANC was 390 cells/μL.

Nasal endoscopy suggested bacterial sinusitis but cultures remained negative. Two days later, similar erythematous plaques appeared on her right eyelid and eyebrow. A repeat chest CT revealed worsening patchy infiltrates in the upper and middle lobes and consolidation versus atelectasis in the lower lobes. Pleural effusions improved with diuresis. Twelve days after chemotherapy was held, she returned with acute, left-sided facial swelling in the setting of neutropenia. Tachypnea persisted despite broad antibiotics and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim for Pneumocystis coverage. Prednisone was started, and the skin lesions improved rapidly. In October 2021, on day 35 of azacitidine plus venetoclax, she developed facial pain and fevers to 38.1 °C. Chest CT revealed new bilateral ground-glass opacities in the upper and middle lobes with consolidative opacities in the lower lobes. Chemotherapy was held on day 4 because of persistent tachycardia and rising oxygen requirements.

His past medical history included sleep apnoea. His medications on presentation were aspirin, clopidogrel, bisoprolol, atorvastatin, and ramipril. He had previously undergone ablation for junctional tachycardia.

Physical examination before the percutaneous coronary intervention was unremarkable.

Coronary angiography revealed a complete occlusion of the distal right coronary artery. Chest radiograph was normal. The right coronary artery was stented without difficulty despite a shepherd's crook configuration of the proximal vessel. Left ventricular ejection fraction was 45% with inferior wall hypokinesis. CT angiography excluded dissection and pulmonary embolism. NT-pro–brain natriuretic peptide was 1784 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography before the procedure showed no valvular abnormalities.

The lesion caused a coaptation defect and a severe eccentric regurgitant jet on transoesophageal echocardiography. Transoesophageal echocardiography identified a 17 mm fine, filamentous mobile lesion attached to the non-coronary cusp. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of infective endocarditis. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient was referred for surgical evaluation.

Colour Doppler interrogation showed no obstruction of the pulmonary veins or of mitral inflow. With each cardiac cycle, the mass protruded closer to the mitral annulus in diastole. After separation from cardiopulmonary bypass, a routine epicardial echocardiogram demonstrated no residual ventricular septal defect and normal ventricular function. An intracardiac thrombus was the primary differential diagnosis for the mass.

She was born full term and had normal developmental milestones.

On examination, she was 114 cm tall (–1.4 SD) and weighed 19.8 kg (–0.8 SD). She had no features of Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy on examination. Her blood pressure was 109/73 mmHg, heart rate 127 beats/min, and SpO2 96% on room air.

Brain CT revealed multiple bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia and frontal cortex. Serum phosphorus was 7.6 mg/dL (normal 3.9–5.8). Intact parathyroid hormone was 343.1 pg/mL (normal 10–65). Laboratory studies showed sodium, glucose, and renal function within normal limits. Electrocardiography demonstrated QT prolongation with QTc 0.496 msec. 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 13.5 ng/mL (normal >20). An interictal electroencephalogram was normal. Ophthalmological examination showed cataracts. Serum calcium was 5.5 mg/dL (normal 8.7–10.2). Thyroid function was normal. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 was 74.3 pg/mL (normal 20–60).

Two months later, she was hospitalized with fever (38.6 °C) and a 3-minute generalized tonic convulsion. Carbamazepine was started on the basis of these findings, and the dyskinesia resolved.

The patient is a 10-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair cat. The cat was evaluated for a 2-day history of anorexia, vomiting and lethargy. The cat had a 1-year history of suspected weight loss and intermittent reduced appetite. The cat had outdoor access.

The cat's body condition score was 4/9. On presentation the cat was lethargic but alert. There was mild diffuse discomfort on abdominal palpation. The cat showed mild tachycardia with a heart rate of 200 beats/min.

Serum biochemistry revealed a severe elevation in serum amyloid A (138.6 µg/ml; RI 0–12). Ultrasonography showed severe gallbladder wall thickening (2.1 mm) consistent with cholecystitis. Blood smear evaluation showed toxic and hyposegmented neutrophils. Serum biochemistry revealed mild hyperglobulinaemia (53 g/l; RI 28–51). Fine-needle aspirates of liver and bile showed rare plasmacytes and lymphocytes in the liver tissue and septic suppurative inflammation in the bile. A second linear hyperechoic structure extended into the duodenal papilla without distal common bile duct dilation. Serum biochemistry revealed moderate hyperbilirubinaemia (14 µmol/l; RI 2–6). Culture of bile yielded Escherichia coli sensitive to marbofloxacin, doxycycline, amoxicillin and sulfatrimethoprim. The complete blood count was within reference intervals. Serum biochemistry revealed a severe elevation in alanine transaminase activity (456 U/l; RI 12–130). In the common bile duct, ultrasound showed a hyperechoic spindle-shaped structure measuring 12 × 2.5 mm with linear interfaces and mild acoustic shadowing.

Repeat biochemistry after 8 days of treatment showed the development of severe ionized hypercalcaemia (1.87 mmol/l; RI 1.1–1.4) with an increased phosphorus concentration. Despite 8 days of treatment, the cat remained lethargic and anorexic. Repeat biochemistry after 8 days of treatment showed persistent elevations in liver enzymes.

The patient is an 18-year-old woman. The patient presented with a 4-year history of severe, global headaches rated 10/10 that had worsened over the past 2 years. She denied trauma, surgery, radiation exposure, fever, cough, or use of osmotic diuretics. Menarche occurred at age 13. She had a weight loss of 10 kg over the past year. Her medications included occasional antacids and analgesics. She reported intermittent epigastric discomfort. She had secondary amenorrhea for 18 months. She woke 10 times per night to urinate. Eighteen months before presentation, she developed polydipsia of approximately 15 L per day with matching polyuria.

On examination, her vital signs were normal. Axillary and pubic hair were normal, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. On examination, her BMI was 16 kg/m2.

Initial laboratory testing showed a urine specific gravity of 1.005 and a random urine osmolality of 150 mOsm/kg. After overnight water deprivation, her serum osmolality rose to 298 mOsm/kg while her urine osmolality remained low at 210 mOsm/kg, with a urine output of 3 L over 8 h and a urine specific gravity of 1.006. Because intravenous desmopressin was unavailable, she was given low-dose oral desmopressin, on which her urine specific gravity normalized to 1.020 and her urine osmolality to 600 mOsm/kg.

Additional laboratory testing showed βhCG of 1.2 mIU/mL, AFP of 7 ng/mL, IgG4 of 28 mg/dL, and soluble IL-2 receptor of 203 U/mL. Brain MRI showed no evidence of intracranial hypertension. Brain MRI showed partial filling of the pituitary fossa by CSF with a flattened pituitary gland measuring 3.68 mm, consistent with a partial empty sella. Anterior pituitary hormones, including TSH, T3, T4, prolactin, and cortisol, were within normal limits. Pelvic ultrasound was normal.

Left ventricular ejection fraction was 65% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Enalapril caused dizziness and worsened fatigue. The patient had difficulty swallowing during the febrile episodes. During the episodes, the patient had enlarged, painful lymph nodes in the cervical and submandibular regions. Headache, muscle pain, and fatigue occurred together with each episode of fever. The patient experienced a sore throat during each febrile episode. During every episode, the patient's temperature reached 38.5–40 °C and the fever persisted for as long as 7 days. The patient's occupation for more than 30 years involved the analysis of black metal. Between the episodes the patient felt completely well and was able to anticipate when the next episode would begin. As a child, the patient had had tonsillitis for which a tonsillectomy was performed.

Histological examination of a biopsied supraclavicular lymph node showed reactive hyperplasia. Testing showed normal procalcitonin, normal immunoglobulin levels, and normal ANA titres. Tests for HIV, CMV, EBV, and other markers of infection returned negative results. The leukocyte count during an episode was 2.94 × 10^9/L. An endoscopic examination of the colon revealed no abnormalities. The neutrophil count during an episode was 3.19 × 10^9/L. Cultures of blood and throat swabs did not grow any organisms. Examination of the pharynx by pharyngoscopy showed inflammation of the pharynx covered with white exudate. On ultrasound, lymph nodes in both cervical, submandibular, and supraclavicular regions were enlarged, with the largest measuring 21 × 6 mm. The CRP measured during an episode was 64 mg/L. On PET-CT, the sigmoid colon showed abnormally high glucose uptake. The serum amyloid A level during an episode was 140 mg/L. The bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetic analysis showed no abnormalities.

The recurrent febrile episodes continued even after the patient received several courses of antibiotic treatment.

The long-term inhaled steroid therapy had led to severe osteoporosis of the spine. He had no hypertension, diabetes, smoking history, or cardiovascular disease. He had chronic left shoulder impingement with limited elbow extension from a remote injury. His medical history included asthma managed with long-term inhaled steroids.

He was classified as ASA class II. Preoperative airway examination showed a Mallampati score of I. Preoperative examination showed no restriction or pain on neck extension, although a note advised careful extension because of the osteoporosis. He weighed 64 kg and had a BMI of 19.8 kg/m2.

Given the mild symptoms and the absence of signs suggesting stroke or a cervical spine complication, no CT or MRI was performed. The 103-minute surgery was uneventful and vital signs remained stable. Shortly after transfer to recovery, painless left arm weakness was noted. Fist closure was normal on the neurological examination 3.5 hours after surgery. There was no headache, altered consciousness, dysarthria, or leg weakness. Vital signs were normal when the weakness was evaluated. Intubation with a conventional laryngoscope in slight neck extension revealed a Cormack–Lehane grade II view. Neurological examination 3.5 hours after surgery showed strength of 2/5 in left shoulder elevation. The patient was positioned supine with a small pillow under the shoulders to produce slight neck extension, with the arms alongside the body. Neurological examination 3.5 hours after surgery showed strength of 4/5 in finger abduction and wrist extension. Anesthesia was induced with fentanyl, propofol, and remifentanil, and no neuromuscular blockers were given. The patient was extubated and transferred to recovery.

The patient is a 47-year-old woman. The patient presented with a two-month history of episodic chest pain, dyspnea, bilateral lower-extremity swelling, cyanosis, and transient loss of consciousness. Two weeks before transfer she noted leg edema. Two years earlier she had undergone an abdominal hysterectomy for uterine fibroids. She had no known risk factors for thromboembolism. Two weeks before transfer she noted the gradual onset of pleuritic chest pain. One day before transfer she developed shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough.

Her heart rate was 110 bpm. Her systolic blood pressure was 70 mm Hg. Her respiratory rate was 34 breaths per minute. At the outside hospital she appeared cyanotic, with dusky skin.

The leukocyte count was 12.9×10³/μL. A head CT scan was normal. Other hematologic, renal, liver, and coagulation studies were within normal limits. Venous duplex ultrasonography revealed a right proximal deep venous thrombosis. Arterial blood gas on 100% oxygen showed pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 506 mm Hg. Serum troponin was normal. An electrocardiogram was normal.

On transfer, a CT scan of the chest identified a 3.1-cm hypodense filling defect traversing the right atrium into the right ventricle. The chest CT showed no pulmonary embolism. Unfractionated heparin was started after the deep venous thrombosis was identified. Pelvic CT revealed a 6.2×3.9-cm lobulated pelvic mass inseparable from the internal iliac vein. Abdominal CT showed distension of the inferior vena cava with a similar-density lesion and subtle linear enhancement. The chest CT also showed small bilateral pleural effusions and atelectasis. Transthoracic echocardiography in the apical four-chamber view demonstrated a 3.5×3.0-cm tissue-density mass filling the right atrium to the plane of the tricuspid annulus.

The patient is a 44-year-old man. The patient presented with acute abdominal pain. The patient had a history of colonic diverticulitis.

On examination, his abdomen was distended with right lower quadrant tenderness.

CT showed a few borderline mesenteric lymph nodes. CT showed asymmetric wall thickening of some ileal loops. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed small-bowel loops dilated up to 4.3 cm in diameter, with a transition point in the mid-lower abdomen concerning for moderate enteric obstruction.

Diagnostic laparoscopy identified a nonperforated Meckel diverticulum in the mid-ileum. The lymphocytes were negative for CD10, Cyclin-D1, CD3, and CD5. In situ hybridization for kappa and lambda showed scattered polyclonal plasma cells. The Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 5%. The reactive germinal centers were BCL-2–negative and BCL-6–positive, with no evidence of follicular colonization by tumor cells. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the lymphocytes were positive for CD20 with weak coexpression of CD43 and positive for BCL-2. Histologic examination of the resected diverticulum showed a true diverticulum lined by intestinal mucosa without ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue. Microscopy revealed extensive infiltration of sheets of small lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm (monocytoid B-cells) forming lymphoepithelial lesions in the mucosa and submucosa and focally involving the serosal adipose tissue. The Meckel diverticulum appeared prominent, inflamed, and indurated at laparoscopy.

A peripheral blood smear subsequently showed schistocytes. She was presumed to have thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and was started on high-dose steroids and daily plasma exchange, and dialysis and mycophenolate mofetil were also initiated. Outpatient dialysis and plasma exchange were continued three times weekly without improvement.

The cut surface of the tumor was firm, tan-gray, and lobulated, measuring 6 × 5.5 × 5 cm, with apparently normal salivary gland tissue at the periphery. The resected mass measured 21.5 × 9 × 6 cm.

MRI of the dorsal spinal cord demonstrated T2-weighted hyperintense lesions extending from T3 to T9, with a probable posterolateral lesion at T7–T8. A whole-body PET scan showed no hypermetabolic cerebral or medullary lesions. He received anti-toxoplasma therapy without corticosteroids and had clinical and radiologic improvement. Over one month, the numbness progressed to involve his entire right lower limb and right hemi-abdomen. CSF PCR assays for JC virus, BK virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, human herpesvirus 6, varicella-zoster virus, and enterovirus were negative. CSF analysis showed 5 cells/μL, protein 58 mg/dL, and glucose 51 mg/dL. Three months after HAART initiation, he reported abrupt onset of right lower-limb numbness. He denied fever or other systemic symptoms. HTLV-I/II serology was negative. CSF PCR for Epstein-Barr virus was positive. He initiated HAART one month after diagnosis. Strength, proprioception, and reflexes in the affected areas were preserved. On examination, there was a distinct sensory level at T9 on the right, with loss of touch and pain sensation below this level. At this time, the CD4+ T-cell count had risen to 128 cells/μL and the plasma HIV RNA had fallen to 121 copies/mL. A follow-up brain CT scan revealed that some prior lesions had improved, others had slightly worsened with ring enhancement and edema, and several new lesions had appeared. CSF Gram and acid-fast stains, microbiological cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and VDRL were negative. CSF lymphocyte phenotyping was normal. On examination, mental status and cranial nerves were normal.

Thoracic radiographs were normal. Abdominal ultrasound performed five days earlier had shown a 5.2 × 5.0 cm round hypoechoic mass in the left lateral liver lobe.

Flow cytometry showed that 15% of the cells were CD45+ MHC class II+ leukocytes lacking lineage markers.

The patient is a 20-year-old woman. The patient had constant right proximal thigh pain that had progressed over 8 years. She had no other medical conditions. The pain required daily NSAIDs, paracetamol, and weak opioids. She had no family history of bone disease. She was on sick leave due to her symptoms. At age 11 she had hip joint pain with an ultrasound-guided aspiration revealing sterile fluid, after which the pain resolved. She had a leg-length discrepancy that was managed with shoe inserts. Six months prior she was hit by a car at knee level, no fracture was diagnosed, and her thigh pain worsened afterward. The pain was somewhat relieved by activity and cold baths. The pain was worse at night.

Leg lengths were slightly unequal but within normal limits. On examination, there were no skin lesions, café au lait spots, erythema, heat, or swelling over the right thigh.

Magnetic resonance imaging and PET–CT showed significant increased cortical thickness of the right femoral diaphysis with partial medullary obliteration and an uneven sclerotic surface. Genetic screening in blood for the GNAS1 R201 mutation and for SQSTM1 mutations was negative. Biochemical bone markers, including alkaline phosphatase, were normal. A Tc-99m bone scan demonstrated increased uptake in most of the right femoral shaft.

Bone biopsy showed no fibrosis, inflammation, alcian positivity, malignancy, or neoplasia. Bone biopsy of the lesion revealed thickened bone trabeculae with preserved lamellar structure and accentuated cement lines.

The patient is a 39-year-old woman. The patient was evaluated for recurrent seizures that began in early 2014. She had had no gastrointestinal symptoms since 2013. Crohn's disease was treated with steroids and mesalazine until 2008 and then with methotrexate (15 mg weekly) through 2016. She noted progressive short-term memory impairment in the weeks before the first seizure. The initial seizure events were dyscognitive and progressed to secondary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She had smoked 25 pack-years. Crohn's disease had been diagnosed in 2006 by ileocolonoscopy. Some weeks before the first seizure, she developed subacute bifrontal headaches.

Initial cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed pleocytosis (14 cells/μl) with negative oligoclonal bands. In August 2014, after a secondarily generalized seizure, MRI showed multiple supratentorial gadolinium-enhancing cortical lesions. Serum levels of interleukin-2 receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme, neopterin, and calcium were normal. An interferon-gamma release assay was negative. In early 2014, a head CT excluded hemorrhage after a transient dyscognitive event was interpreted as a transient ischemic attack. Bronchoalveolar lavage and chest CT were normal. ANCA, ANA, and antiphospholipid antibody studies were normal.

Neuropsychological testing showed depressive symptoms with attentional, executive, and memory deficits. Repeat CSF analysis in August 2016 showed pleocytosis (8 cells/μl), elevated protein, and now positive oligoclonal bands. In May 2015, her husband observed a transient personality change with disinhibited behavior, which did not recur. Two months after the August 2014 MRI, a follow-up MRI demonstrated progression of the cortical lesions. In September 2016, CSF testing for Borrelia burgdorferi, Treponema pallidum, HSV-1/2, VZV, Tropheryma whipplei, and HIV was negative. After methotrexate was supplemented with prednisolone, the lesion load was stable on MRI in February 2015. Extensive serologic and CSF testing for neural autoantibodies, including paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis panels, was negative. Fluorescein angiography of the retina excluded small-vessel vasculitis or Susac's syndrome.

Mammography revealed a high-density mass with clustered microcalcifications in the inferior lateral right breast. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the breast lesion yielded class V cells, consistent with malignancy.

Abdominal ultrasound performed as part of staging demonstrated a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with internal blood flow signals arising from the splenic periphery. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 40-mm well-circumscribed splenic lesion with less enhancement than the surrounding parenchyma in the arterial and portal phases, becoming isodense in the delayed phase. Given the inability to establish a definitive diagnosis noninvasively, the decision was made to perform a partial mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy and a simultaneous laparoscopic splenectomy for therapeutic diagnosis. PET-CT showed no significant FDG uptake in the splenic lesion. MRI of the abdomen revealed a lesion isointense to the spleen on T1- and T2-weighted images, with slow centripetal enhancement reaching parity with the spleen at 10 minutes post-contrast.

The patient is an 8-year-old girl. The patient presented with a 10-day history of left-sided otalgia, otorrhea, and ipsilateral hearing loss. On the day of admission she noted binocular diplopia and strabismus. She did not have headache. She did not have ocular pain. She vomited the night before presentation. Her past medical history was unremarkable. She had taken paracetamol and ibuprofen regularly during her illness. She had a single day of fever on day 4 of her illness.

On examination her temperature was 38.0°C. Neurologic examination was notable for an ipsilateral abducens nerve palsy. Meningeal signs were absent. Otoscopic examination showed a suppurative left-sided acute otitis media. Tuning-fork testing demonstrated bilateral conductive hearing loss. Trigeminal sensation was intact. There were no other focal deficits on neurologic examination.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head demonstrated ipsilateral septic cavernous sinus thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head demonstrated left mastoiditis and left petrous apicitis (apical petrositis). The C-reactive protein level was 88.8 mg/L. The white blood cell count was 26,200/µL with 93.4% neutrophils. Renal function and coagulation studies were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head demonstrated infectious arteritis with stenosis of the internal carotid artery.

MRI showed enhancement and swelling of the cavernous sinus. MRI confirmed diffuse enhancement of the left mastoid air cells and petrous apex with extraosseous extension to the adjacent dura. MRI showed approximately 50% stenosis of the petrous, lacerum, and cavernous segments of the internal carotid artery.

He later developed bilateral foot drop. He had mild difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a low chair.

Pinprick and light-touch sensation were reduced in a length-dependent distribution. Ankle inversion and eversion strength were 4/5. Vibration and proprioception were intact. Reflexes were 1+ in the upper limbs and absent at the knees and ankles. On examination, there was no obvious muscle atrophy. He had difficulty with plantar flexion when standing on his toes. Manual strength testing showed ankle dorsiflexion of 2/5 on the right and 4–/5 on the left. Hip girdle and thigh strength were 5/5.

A 30-gene Charcot–Marie–Tooth panel was negative. The biceps brachii and vastus lateralis were normal on needle EMG. Nerve conduction studies revealed mildly reduced peroneal and tibial CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities, and sensory nerve conduction studies were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed normal CBC, vitamin B12, TSH, serum protein electrophoresis, hemoglobin A1c, paraneoplastic antibodies, and renal and liver function tests. Creatine kinase was mildly elevated at 508 U/L. Prominent myotonic discharges were noted in several muscles on needle EMG. Needle EMG demonstrated fibrillations, positive sharp waves, and polyphasic, long-duration motor-unit potentials with reduced recruitment in the tibialis anterior (most prominent) and gastrocnemius.

Because EMG showed myotonic potentials, genetic testing for myotonic dystrophy types 1 and 2 was performed and was negative.

He denied neck pain, sensory changes, autonomic symptoms, and bowel or bladder dysfunction. His symptoms progressed over the first 3 years but have been static since then. After 2 years of right-hand symptoms, he began to notice tremors in his left hand without accompanying weakness. Over the same period, he observed a tremor and progressive reduction in muscle bulk of his right hand. There was no history of trauma, surgery, medication use, vaccination, or toxin exposure. He had no family history of neurologic disease.

Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally and Hoffman signs were absent. Tone was reduced around the right elbow and wrist. Muscle strength on the Medical Research Council scale was 2/5 in the right interossei, 3/5 in right wrist flexion and extension, and 4/5 in right elbow flexion and extension, while left upper-limb strength was normal. Minipolymyoclonus was present in the fingers bilaterally, more pronounced on the right. Motor examination showed atrophy of the right hand, most prominently in the first dorsal interosseous, with sparing of the brachioradialis. Deep-tendon reflexes were symmetrical and normal except for a brisk right supinator response. Neurologic examination revealed normal cranial nerves, coordination, sensation, and gait.

Nerve conduction studies demonstrated motor axonal neuropathy with reduced compound motor action potentials in the right median and ulnar nerves, with normal findings on the left. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, thyroid function, inflammatory markers, creatine phosphokinase, viral serologies, and autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA), were within normal limits. A cervical spine radiograph was unremarkable. Needle EMG showed neurogenic discharges with fibrillations and fasciculations in bilateral first dorsal interossei and the right biceps and triceps.

Cervical spine MRI, including flexion T1-weighted contrast and neutral T2-weighted sequences, showed no dural enhancement, no anterior displacement of the posterior dural sac, and no cord atrophy or signal abnormality. A prior cervical spine MRI performed 2 years earlier was also normal.

The WBC count was 9,000/µL with 28% eosinophils (absolute count 2520/µL). Chest X-ray showed no infiltrates or adenopathy. Peripheral smear demonstrated mature-appearing eosinophils without atypia. Stool PCR panel was negative for bacterial and viral pathogens, and ova and parasites were negative. Review of her medications excluded drug-induced eosinophilia. Lipase was 2831 IU/L, and it had been 2415 IU/L five days earlier. HIV test was negative and IgG4 was 40 mg/dL (normal <86).

Helicobacter pylori testing was negative, and no villous abnormality, cryptitis, or crypt abscesses were identified.

Ten days before this presentation he had been admitted for a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage that was managed nonoperatively, and he had been discharged after 3 days on analgesics and an anticonvulsant.

He had dry mucous membranes and visible skin-fold dehydration. His weight was 65 kg, down from 71 kg 10 days earlier. His skin was mottled and his extremities were cool. He was tachypneic. He was hypotensive, with a blood pressure of 74/30 mm Hg. He was tachycardic, with a heart rate of 135 bpm. His urine output was low at 0.3 mL/kg/h. On examination he was alert, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15.

Plasma osmolality was low at 254 mmol/kg H₂O. Laboratory studies showed hypochloremia, with a serum chloride of 54 mEq/L. Arterial blood gas analysis showed metabolic alkalosis.

After infusion of 30 mL/kg of saline he remained hypotensive and required norepinephrine. Six hours later his blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, his lactate had fallen to 1.8 mmol/L, and his urine output had improved.

Physical examination revealed a solitary plaque on the right temple without other skin lesions. No systemic abnormalities were found on physical examination.

The cells had abundant, finely granulated cytoplasm and slight nuclear polymorphism. The serum tryptase level was normal at 2.9 μg/L (normal <11.4 μg/L). Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD117, tryptase, and MiTF. Scattered spindle-shaped and bilobed or multilobed nuclei were present in the biopsy. CD2 immunostaining was negative. A punch biopsy of the lesion revealed diffuse sheets of epithelioid cells in the dermis without epidermal involvement. Giemsa stain highlighted metachromatic granules in the cells. Mitotic activity in the biopsy was low, with up to 1 mitotic figure/mm2. A few lesional cells were positive for CD25. CD30 showed heterogeneous positivity on immunohistochemistry. Next-generation sequencing of the lesion showed no KIT mutations in exons 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, or 17.

No clinical or imaging evidence of systemic disease was found. The excision specimen contained up to 9 mitotic figures/mm2. CD117 and tryptase staining demonstrated small clusters of mast cells extending into the resection margin. The excision specimen showed histopathologic features similar to the biopsy but with increased nuclear pleomorphism. The Ki-67 index of the excised lesion was 29.5%. In July 2014, the lesion was excised.

The team elected to observe the ascending aortic findings without surgical intervention.

Mild tenderness was noted near the L4 spinous process. The mass compressed but did not infiltrate the sacrum, and the adjacent bone showed compressive sclerosis without destruction. Noncontrast attenuation of the mass was 55 HU, with heterogeneous enhancement measuring 61–85 HU in the arterial phase and 67–95 HU in the venous phase. Routine tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA, AFP, NSE, and others) were within normal limits. A central low-density area was present within the mass on CT. Contrast-enhanced CT of the lumbosacral region revealed a well-demarcated, homogeneous soft-tissue mass measuring 3.2 × 7.5 cm within the right multifidus muscle.

MRI showed an intramuscular lesion extending from L4 to S3. STIR images demonstrated slightly hyperintense signal with patchy low-signal foci. Post-contrast MRI sequences revealed heterogeneous enhancement with lamellar nonenhancing regions. The tumor showed marked nuclear pleomorphism with prominent nucleoli and approximately 2 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. At surgery, the tumor was found within the right multifidus muscle, firm and poorly circumscribed, infiltrating surrounding muscle but without bone destruction. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for S100 protein, SOX-10, MDM2, and Bcl-2. There was no definite invasion of nerves, vessels, or bone on histology. On T1-weighted images, the mass was isointense to muscle with patchy hypointense areas. The Ki-67 proliferation index exceeded 10%. Grossly, the resected tumor measured 7.5 cm and was yellowish-gray and slightly firm. Immunohistochemical stains were negative for Desmin, MyoD1, Myogenin, CD99, Synaptophysin, CK-pan, CD34, ERG, and CD163.

The patient is a 71-year-old man. He presented with a 2-day history of right wrist and hand pain, tenderness, and swelling. Eighteen days before presentation, he had been admitted for COVID-19 pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula and bilevel positive-pressure ventilation. During that ICU stay, he also had multiple venous blood draws and peripheral IV placements. He had a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. His medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, carvedilol, lisinopril, and sublingual nitroglycerin as needed. He reported easy bruising and bleeding. He was receiving therapeutic enoxaparin 90 mg subcutaneously twice daily. During a 16-day ICU stay at the referring hospital, he underwent frequent arterial blood gas sampling from both radial arteries. He was transferred from a long-term acute care facility. He reported fatigue, shortness of breath, and generalized weakness. He never had an indwelling arterial line during his ICU stay.

Sensation and motor strength were intact in the right hand. Examination revealed diffuse bilateral inspiratory crackles. On admission, his respiratory rate was 30 breaths/min and his oxygen saturation was 88% on 10 L nasal cannula. Radial and ulnar pulses were palpable. Examination revealed anasarca. On admission, his blood pressure was 158/70 mm Hg and his heart rate was 104 beats/min. Examination revealed mild tenderness and swelling of the right wrist and hand with bruising on the volar wrist. The right fingers felt cool on examination. On admission, his temperature was 96.7°F.

The admission chest radiograph showed bilateral infiltrates consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia. Electrolytes and renal function were normal.

She had no history of trauma, cosmetic lip tattooing, or burns. She had intermittent bronchitis that was treated with a corticosteroid nasal spray. She had no known immunodeficiency. She had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or opium use.

The lip ulcer discharged fluid when pressed. There was no lymphadenopathy. She was afebrile. On examination, there was an ill-demarcated, tender, thick-crusted ulcer measuring 3 × 1 cm on the lower lip. The remainder of her examination was unremarkable. There were no signs of onychomycosis or interdigital intertrigo.

Despite local wound care, topical antifungal and antimicrobial therapies, and empiric immunosuppressive and antibiotic treatments, the ulcer worsened. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for immunobullous diseases. Two incisional biopsies of the lip lesion showed parakeratotic hyperkeratosis, severe acanthosis, spongiosis, exocytosis of inflammatory cells in the epidermis, and a mixed dermal infiltrate without evidence of malignant transformation. The nitroblue tetrazolium test was normal. A direct smear for leishmaniasis was negative.

She was treated empirically with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ceftriaxone. On day 17, she redeveloped fever, headache, nausea, and vomiting. CSF cultures grew hemolytic streptococcus.

Her medical history was notable for nonspecific joint disease managed with low-dose prednisone and methotrexate.

Slit-lamp examination showed nuclear sclerotic cataracts in both eyes, graded 2+ in the right eye and 1+ in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination revealed mild vessel attenuation in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination revealed 0.5+ vitreous haze in both eyes. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 13 mm Hg in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination showed no cell or flare in either eye.

Antinuclear antibody testing was positive at a titer of 1:80. Complete blood count showed leukocytosis with a white cell count of 11.6 K/µL. Spectral-domain OCT showed preserved foveal contour without subretinal or intraretinal fluid. Initial laboratory tests including liver function, basic metabolic panel, hemoglobin A1c, angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, QuantiFERON, syphilis serologies, and anti-dsDNA, together with chest radiography, were within normal limits. Wide-angle fluorescein angiography demonstrated mild bilateral peripheral perivascular leakage. Complete blood count showed anemia with hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dL, compared with 10.2 g/dL one year earlier.

Methotrexate was discontinued and the patient was started on mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg twice daily and prednisone 20 mg daily. Two months later, repeat fluorescein angiography showed worsening peripheral perivascular leakage. Two months later, visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye.
